body:
**Requested by the user, 2026-11-12 (filed by an agent). The maintainer reviews the scope before any work starts.** It carries `needs-research`, so Pick never takes it for code. Once the questions below are settled, it gets the usual concrete sub-issues.

## The idea
A post option, **Explain G-code** (yes/no, default **no**), that adds a short comment to every block saying what it does. For example:

```
G20 G17 G90 G91.1 G94 G40 G49 G80 (INCH, XY PLANE, ABSOLUTE, ARC CENTERS INCREMENTAL, FEED PER MINUTE, CUTTER COMP OFF, TOOL LENGTH OFF, CYCLES OFF)
G64 P0.001 (PATH BLENDING, 0.001 IN TOLERANCE)
G99 (CANNED CYCLE RETURNS TO R PLANE)
G73 X0.7874 Y0.3937 Z-0.9449 R0 Q0.7087 F3.94 (CHIP-BREAK PECK DRILL TO Z-0.9449, 0.7087 PECKS)
G53 G0 Z0 (RAPID TO MACHINE Z HOME)
M30 (END OF PROGRAM, REWIND)
```

It helps users learning G-code, makes a posted program easier to check by eye before it runs (the Hub reviews showed how useful that is), and helps when someone hand-edits a program at the control.

## Open questions for the maintainer
1. **Where the option lives:** a per-post property (each `.cps` declares it), a machine-file setting, a document/setup post setting, or all of these with an order of precedence? Is it also in the post dialog and over MCP?
2. **Scope:** every post, or the Tormach/LinuxCNC family first? Each dialect has its own comment syntax and limits: `( )` versus `;`, Fanuc-family line and comment length limits, controls that drop or reject long comments, and Heidenhain conversational has no G words at all.
3. **Safety:** comments must stay inert. On PathPilot/LinuxCNC a comment that begins with MSG, DEBUG, PRINT, LOG, PY, etc. is executed, and the existing `note()` guard has to cover these too. No comment may change program behaviour, and a golden should check that a program with and without the option gives byte-identical motion once comments are stripped.
4. **Wording source:** the comment text must be original, written from the public G-code references (RS-274/ISO 6983, LinuxCNC docs, and the control makers' public manuals), never copied from another product's output.
5. **Size:** a much longer program file on controls with little memory. Should the post warn, or refuse, on a machine file that states a program size limit?
6. **Detail level:** one comment per block, or a modal-change-only mode that comments a word only when it changes?

## Done means (for this umbrella)
The questions are answered in comments and the sub-issues are filed, each with `P*`, `effort:*` and `area:*`. Then this umbrella is closed.

body:
**Found in a PathPilot Hub run (770MX sim, v2.14.4, 2026-11-12).** The Tormach golden `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/tormach/drill_peck.nc` (and its inch twin) alarms at line 9:

```
G73: Cannot feed with zero feed rate
  in drill_peck_inch.nc: line 9: G73 X0.7874 Y0.3937 Z-0.9449 R0 Q0.7087
```

**Cause.** The golden is posted from the CL fixture `drill_peck.cl`. Its `; CYCLE Peck ...` record has no feed, and the fixture has no tool record. `CycleRec::props` passes `FeedRate: null`. `tormach.cps` `onCycle` then calls `fw(p.FeedRate)`, which writes nothing, and posts a G73 with no F. The same fixtures also post no `T.. M6`, `S..` or `M3`. So `contour_plate_with_hole.nc` cuts its G1/G2/G3 moves with the spindle never started. In Hub that showed as T0 and spindle 0 rpm, and it still ran to M30.

**Why it matters.** A real CamCraft program carries the tool's feed and spindle, so this has not been seen from the GUI. But the post fails open. Under the Prime Directive, a stream that asks for a feed cycle without a feed, or for a cut with no spindle on, should be refused by name and not posted. On a control that keeps a modal F from an earlier block, a missing F on a canned cycle drills at whatever feed was last in force.

**Done means:**
- `tormach.cps`, and every post with the same `fw()` pattern on cycles, refuses a canned cycle whose `FeedRate` is missing or not positive, by name.
- A feed move (G1/G2/G3, or a cycle) before any spindle start is refused by name. Spindleless dialects (plasma, laser) are exempt.
- The golden fixtures that post to Tormach state a tool, spindle and feed, so the Tormach goldens are real runnable programs. The goldens are regenerated, and the change is listed in the PR.
- Pinning tests: a cycle with no feed is refused; a cut with no spindle start is refused.

body:
Seen on 2026-11-12, a day with about 50 merges: `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one integer that every process PR increments in its own branch. Each time one of them merges, every other open process PR either conflicts on that one line (GitHub shows CONFLICTING and the PR drops out of a merge run) or, worse, carries the SAME new number and merges cleanly - two process changes then share one number and a fork that already synced at it never pulls the second (it happened with #1117 and #930 at 17; fixed by the extra bump PR #1142). Today #965, #967, #972, #1033, #1024, #1100, #1116 and #1151 all had to be renumbered by hand, some more than once.

The law today (AGENTS.md "Process changes bump PROCESS_VERSION"): the PR increments the number; "whichever merges second takes the next number when it merges main".

Proposal to decide (maintainer): the number is not written in the PR at all. A process PR only says in its body "process change: yes" (the reviewer checks that instead of the bump); the merging session increments `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` right after the merge in a one-line follow-up PR (or the merge tooling does: `cargo xtask process-bump`), and posts the #681 announcement with that number. One writer, no conflicts, no shared numbers. Alternatives: derive the version from the count of merge commits touching the process paths (no file at all), or keep the file and make `.gitattributes` resolve it with a custom "max + 1" merge driver (needs local git config on every clone, so probably not).

Done means: the chosen rule is in AGENTS.md (and the review-prs / merge-ready skills), two process PRs open at once no longer conflict with each other, and two of them can never land on the same number; `PROCESS_VERSION` bumped and announced for this change itself.

labels.name: bug

body:
Found while working #984.

**What happens:** the same commit plans the same part differently on two platforms. `app pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (release) on ecb54b7f:

| platform | rings levels | moves / planar / arcs |
|---|---|---|
| Windows (the #850 measure, PR #865) | Z 20.000 | 5530 / 5497 / 600 |
| macOS, Apple silicon (Homebrew rustc 1.99.1) | Z 20.000 (crossing at -2.33, -2.78) | 5786 / 5753 / 651 |

macOS is deterministic run to run, so it is not hash-map order. Rust does not contract `a*b+c` into FMA unless asked, so the most likely cause is the platform libm: `f64::sin`, `cos`, `atan2`, `hypot`, `exp`, `powf` call the system math library (MSVC CRT, glibc, Apple libm), which are not correctly rounded and differ in the last place. The STEP tessellation and the adaptive planner both use them, and the planner's crossing and acceptance tests are knife edges a 16 nm change flips (#882, #982). Not yet confirmed which call sites diverge, and not run on Linux.

**Why it matters:** a toolpath (and so the posted G-code) for the same part, tool and parameters depends on the OS the user runs. Every output is still verified and a crossing plan is refused by name, so this is not a gouge; but golden counts and exact plan pins cannot hold across platforms, and a user can see a different path from the same project file on two machines.

**Possible directions (open):** route the geometry and planner transcendental calls through a pure-Rust deterministic libm (the `libm` crate is already in Cargo.lock) so every platform rounds the same; or make the planner's decisions robust to sub-micron perturbation (#882, #982). Either changes toolpaths and needs every adaptive fixture re-measured.

Done means: the cause is confirmed on a second platform (Windows or Linux run of the bore test, plus which calls diverge), and either the output is made platform-identical with goldens re-measured, or the decision not to is recorded.

Refs #984, #882, #982.

body:
Part of #894.

A thread mill is not centre-cutting, and the thread-milling ride (`machining2d::thread_ride`) feeds it down the hole's axis before the first lead-in arc. That is air only if an earlier operation opened the hole. Nothing checks it: the `Thread` operation generates and verifies clean on a part whose hole is modelled, even when the program holds no drilling operation before it and the stock at the hole is solid. The gouge laws read the part (the hole is in the model), so they see nothing; the centre-cutting audit (`operation::plunge_solid`, `camcraft_motion::plunge_law`) is not asked for this kind, and it reads the raw stock, which would refuse every thread.

**Effect:** forget the tap drill and the program plunges a thread mill into solid metal at plunge feed - a broken cutter, with no finding at generate, at verify or at the post gate.

**Fix sketch:** read the stock the setup's earlier operations leave standing (the prior grid the drilling laws already read, `operation::drill_prior`) under each threaded hole: the tool's full cylinder down the axis and the first pass's lead-in must fall through air. Refuse by name at generate ("the hole at (x, y) is not drilled yet - add a drilling operation before the thread") and digest the program ahead in the stamp, so reordering the operations marks the thread Stale.

**Done means:** a Thread operation with no drilled hole under it is refused by name; the same operation after a Drill of at least the tool's diameter generates; moving the Drill after the Thread turns it Stale and refuses; pinned by an app test. The milled `Bore` ride's axis entry gets the same reading or its own issue.

title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

title: Adaptive growth planner: the ring opening is quadratic in outline vertices - one level of the user's STEP bore grows for ~200 s

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Found while reworking #850 (PR #865).

**What happens:** app `pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (heavy lane, `testdata/models/Milling-test.step`). On main, one level's growth plan spends **~200 s in release** in `adaptive/grow.rs`: 33 revolutions, 157 trial steps, about 1.3 s per trial.

**Where the time goes** (local probe, release):
- 99 % of it is `rings::open`, the morphological opening: two `offset_fine` calls at `ARC_TOL` 2.5e-4 mm per trial, plus one per revolution for `whole`.
- The stock walk takes 0.6 s.
- The cleared-area offset and the intersect take 0.2 s each.

The opening's cost grows about with the **square** of the ring's vertex count. Measured cost per (vertices per trial)^2:

| fixture | vertices per trial | ns per (vertices)^2 |
|---|---|---|
| 60 x 14 slot | ~290 | ~63 |
| 60 x 40 island | ~700 | ~105 |
| the bore (fine STEP tessellation) | ~4,700 | ~58 |

So a finely tessellated outline turns a 33-revolution plan into minutes.

**Why it is not bounded:** #850's budget cannot refuse it without changing a plan that finishes on main. Measured on any time-faithful unit, the bore is the most expensive plan of all, so it stays law 2's (length) alone. See `docs/decisions/850-adaptive-geometry-budget.md`.

**Options:**
- Simplify the cleared area and the ring to the planner's working tolerance before the opening. Douglas-Peucker at the `MERGE` / `ARC_TOL` scale would remove the boolean engine's arc-tolerance vertices that say nothing about the shape.
- An opening that does not re-tessellate every convex vertex at `ARC_TOL`.
- An incremental opening.

Each option changes toolpaths: under the safety floor, with every adaptive fixture re-measured.

**Done means:** the bore's growth level plans in seconds (stated bound, release and debug) with the load, crossing and kink laws held. Every adaptive fixture's change is measured and named in the PR.

Related: #850, #44, #845.

body:
**What happens**

The 3-2-1 alignment (#187) and `SetWcsOrigin` can set a rotated work offset, and the viewport shows the rotated frame — but nothing downstream machines in it:

- Toolpaths generate in world axes; only the offset's translation (`wcs_context` → `OriginX/Y/Z`) reaches the record stream (`posting_wcs_rotation.rs`).
- Heights / machining planes stay world-Z.
- The post refuses a rotated offset by name (#315, shipped in v0.15.0) — correct and safe, but by then the user has built a state the whole page presented as valid: the display shows a frame the CAM does not machine.

User-reported on main 5fd45923: align a setup's WCS with 3-2-1 on a turned part → the WCS is right in the display, toolpath and machining plane do not follow. Not yet pinned by a test.

**Fix (step 3 of #315, owed)**

Carry the rotation end-to-end, as a user parameter with a default:

- generation and heights compute in the offset's frame, so toolpath and machining planes follow the alignment, and
- the post either bakes rotated coordinates into the program or emits the control's own rotation where the machine declares it (Fanuc G68 / G68.2, Siemens CYCLE800 / ROT, Heidenhain PLANE / CYCL 10 — public control documentation only; a G54 register is translation only on every control).

Interim, if the full carry is not taken at once: the 3-2-1 flow should say at alignment time that a rotated offset will not post (the refusal currently arrives only at the post gate), or steer to part alignment (#330, #746).

**Done means**

A part aligned with a rotated work offset machines in that frame: toolpath, height planes and posted program all carry the same rotation, pinned against a hand-computed program — or the alignment refuses with a clear message before any toolpath exists. Never a display that shows a frame nothing machines.

**Related**: #315 (the shipped refusal), #187 (3-2-1 alignment), #330 / #746 (part alignment, the alternative path), #701 (will create rotated offsets from feature roles and needs this to machine them).

body:
**What's missing:** a document tool can be added over MCP (`add_tool`), but it can't be edited or deleted. The tool editor's commands are `ChangeTool` (replace the definition, so ops on the tool turn stale) and `DeleteTool` (remove it; undo restores its number and body), both in `crates/app/src/commands/tool.rs`. A headless agent that needs a longer stickout, a different flute count or another rpm has to add a second tool under a new name and re-point every op with `set_tool`. A tool added by mistake can only go by `undo`.

**Neighbour that works:** `edit_operation { name, params }` applies a JSON merge patch over an op's fields, refuses an unknown field by name, and runs `EditOperationParams` (`crates/app/src/mcp/edit.rs`).

**Done means:**
- `edit_tool { name, definition }` applies a JSON merge patch over the tool's `get_job` definition, refuses an unknown field by name, and runs `ChangeTool` through `env.history`, one undo step. The command's own refusals come back as tool errors: non-finite or non-positive numbers, a retype the tool law refuses for an op using the tool, a body that no longer fits.
- `delete_tool { name }` runs `DeleteTool`, one undo step. The reply names any operations that still use the tool.
- In-process JSON-RPC tests pin both: an edit makes the op stale, undo restores it, and the refusals are named. They also cover what verify and post do once a used tool is gone.

body:
Add machine definitions, and the post they need, for Sienci Labs' AltMill CNC routers, driven by the SLB-EXT controller. **There are three sizes:**

| | AltMill 2×4 | AltMill 4×4 | AltMill 4×8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Work area (X × Y) | ~25 × 49 in | ~49 × 49 in (1265 × 1251 mm) | ~49.8 × 104 in (1265 × 2640 mm) |
| Z travel | ~5.5 in | ~5.5 in (one page: 174 mm) | ~210 mm |
| Max cutting speed | ~590-600 IPM | ~590-600 IPM | ~1,000 IPM Y, ~590 IPM X |
| Spindle | none included: 80 mm mount; optional 2.2 kW ER20 spindle, or the 2.2 kW ATC spindle | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |
| Rotary (optional) | Vortex rotary axis on the SLB-EXT's A output | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |
| Motion | NEMA 23 closed-loop steppers | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |

The figures come from Sienci's product and resources pages, which disagree with each other in places (the 4×4's Z: 5.5 in vs 174 mm; X and Y speeds). Confirm each figure against Sienci's current spec page or manual before committing a `.mch` (see Done means).

**Controller:** the SLB-EXT is a 32-bit board running **grblHAL**, usually driven by Sienci's gSender. That makes this post a grblHAL dialect, built on the grblHAL post in #710 (PR #715) rather than written from scratch.

**No new post file.** The AltMill machine files use `grblhal.cps` from #710, the way all the Tormach mills share `tormach.cps`. A separate `altmill.cps` is added only if something below cannot be a machine-file setting or a grblHAL post option. As of PR #715, the grblHAL post already does what an ATC needs: a plain `T<n> M6` on a line of its own, no G49 (the controller's measured tool length is kept), a `G53 G0 Z` lift when the machine file states `safe_retract` (the AltMill homes), and the first move after a change goes to XY before Z.

**Requirements** (on the machine files, or as small additions to the grblHAL post):
- **Tool change:** the most AltMill-specific part. The post must not depend on the sender: AltMill owners use gSender, and also alternatives such as ncSender. Two modes:
  - *Manual*: the sender intercepts `M6` and runs its own tool-change routine (pause, probe, and so on).
  - *ATC (firmware-handled)*: a `TC.macro` on the SLB-EXT runs `M6 Tn` inside grblHAL, which is transparent to the sender. This covers Sienci's ATC spindle and the **RapidChange ATC** ([rcatc-scripts-grblhal](https://github.com/greilick-industries/rcatc-scripts-grblhal): `TC.macro` runs on every `M6` with a valid tool, settings in `P200.macro`, grblHAL core 20240506 or newer).
  - In both modes the post emits a plain `M6 Tn` on a line of its own, as #710 already plans, with the length offset on the next line. It adds no sender-specific comments or macros, because some gSender versions reportedly rewrite `M6T1` even in passthrough.
  - A post option picks manual or ATC. With ATC, the machine file states the rack's pocket count and which tool numbers it holds, and any other tool is a manual change or a refusal by name. The tool length comes from the ATC's own measurement, so the post does not ask for a manual touch-off after an ATC change.
- **Units:** most AltMill users work in inches. The post honours G20/G21 from the setup and never mixes them.
- **Spindle:** the spindle is bought separately, so the machine file carries a default spindle (the 2.2 kW ER20, 24,000 rpm max, to be checked against Sienci's kit page) that the user can change. `S` words are clamped to the stated range, or refused by name if out of range.
- **Rotary (Vortex):** an A-axis rotary along X on the SLB-EXT's dedicated A output (closed-loop Vortex, gSender's "4th Axis Mode"). The older "Rotary Mode", which drives the rotary through the Y output, is not supported and is refused by name. Indexing and wrapping follow #714 and wait on it.
- **Out of scope:** laser (LaserBeam) and plasma add-ons.

**Done means:**
- `assets/machines/sienci-altmill-2x4.mch`, `sienci-altmill-4x4.mch` and `sienci-altmill-4x8.mch` exist, with travels, axis speeds, the default spindle and the rotary option. Every figure is sourced from Sienci's spec page or manual and cited in the decision file.
- All three are registered in `posting::MACHINES`, with tests in the style of the Tormach machine tests.
- The AltMill machines post through `grblhal.cps`, with goldens under `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/grblhal/` for a small pocket with a tool change on an AltMill machine, in both inch and mm. With an ATC rack stated, a tool outside the rack is handled as above. Any change needed in `grblhal.cps` keeps its existing goldens byte-exact.
- Without #714, any A word is refused by name. Once #714 lands, the Vortex is covered by its indexing goldens.
- The post passes a sender run and a real-machine dry run before it is trusted. I have an AltMill with an SLB-EXT, a RapidChange ATC and ncSender, and can run the goldens on that setup (ATC mode, ncSender).

Depends on: #710 (grblHAL post). Related: #714 (grblHAL 4th axis), #707 (similar machine + post request).

body:
Proposed by the maintainer (filed by an agent), 2026-11-10. **Paused (`P?`) for the maintainer's review**; nothing is picked up until he sets a priority.

## Goal
A public site on GitHub Pages with:
1. **Documentation** (user guide plus developer and architecture docs), generated with **[Zola](https://www.getzola.org/)** (a single binary static site generator, Markdown content, Tera templates, no Node toolchain).
2. **CamCraft in the browser:** the WASM build of the app, published alongside the docs, so a release can be tried without installing anything.

## How it should work
- **Source:** a Zola project in the repo (e.g. `site/`: `config.toml`, `content/`, `templates/`, `static/`). The docs content lives there as Markdown. Existing material is reused where it fits (README sections, `docs/` design notes, release notes).
- **Output folder:** Zola builds into one folder that Pages picks up. Options to decide in review: the `public/` output deployed by the Pages "GitHub Actions" source, or a `gh-pages` branch / `docs/` folder. The site is **regenerated from scratch each release** (no incremental state, no hand-edited output in git).
- **Part of the release cycle:** generating and publishing the site is a step of the minor/major cut (AGENTS.md "A cut goes PR review -> merge to main -> tag"), run on the tagged tree. If it runs on GitHub, it goes in the existing tag-triggered `release.yml`. **No new `push`/`pull_request`/`schedule` trigger** (AGENTS.md Actions budget). It can also be built locally (`zola build`) for previews.
- **Versioned content:** the site shows the version it was built from. Each release overwrites the previous site (one live version); older versions stay in the GitHub releases.
- **WASM app:** the release step builds the app for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (the web build from #31), bundles it (e.g. `wasm-bindgen` + a small loader page, or `trunk`), and places it under the site (e.g. `/app/`), so `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/app/` runs CamCraft in the browser. It is linked from the docs front page with a note on what works in the browser and what doesn't (file access, GPU features).

## Open questions (for the review)
- Pages source: Actions-deployed `public/` vs a branch/folder? (Actions deploy keeps generated files out of git.)
- WASM readiness: #31 says only geometry, CL and post build for wasm32 today. Does this issue wait for #31, or ship docs first and add `/app/` when #31 lands?
- Content scope for the first cut: user guide only, or the developer/architecture section too?
- Relation to #291 (needs-research, which proposed mdBook): this issue picks Zola. On approval, #291's research is folded in here, or #291 is closed as superseded.
- Actions minutes: building the WASM app and the site on the tag run adds billed minutes. Measure and keep it within the budget.

## Done means (once approved and broken down)
- A Zola site in the repo builds locally with `zola build`.
- The release cycle regenerates and publishes it to GitHub Pages at each minor/major cut, with no new CI triggers.
- The published site carries the version and links to the release downloads.
- The WASM build of CamCraft is published under the site and loads in a current browser (once #31 makes the UI build for wasm32).
- AGENTS.md's release steps name the site step.

Related: #291 (documentation site, mdBook proposal), #31 (app and UI on wasm), #72 (release compile targets).

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.
